rv.q: Diamond has something special here and her Broadway debut is a refreshing chance to scrutinize an elite slice of America.
Stick Fly is a warmly written family drama that benefits from committed performances by its talented cast, even if the play itself feels somewhat overstuffed with incident and theme.
That’s what the playwright does to her characters in “Stick Fly.”
In spite of a few sincere performances, "Stick Fly" is utterly derivative of better-known family dramas and dependent on shock value.
Under Kenny Leon’s sluggish direction, the women win the contest, at least in the acting department.
This overstuffed but lively comedy-drama signifies a departure for Broadway in its depiction of generational conflict among a well-to-do contemporary African-American family.
But at heart this is a sitcom-soap hybrid that often serves to show how wealthy dysfunctional African American families can be every bit as tiresome and self-involved as their white counterparts.
Marin Ireland and Peter Kim are the hapless couple who seem way too smart for this flat-footed silliness.
But too often it settles for raised voices and shocking twists and the gasps and clucks that they'll elicit from the audience.
I can't call Lydia R. Diamond's 'Stick Fly' a good play, not with its penchant for overripe secrets, melodramatic revelations, and lazy plotting.
To the show's credit, it's never dull, but amid all the commotion and numerous revelations over two and a half hours, the play doesn't seem to go anywhere.
If not for the superb actors and Leon's fiercely committed treatment of them, the gorgeously messy plot could not keep the play from being a snoozer.
While the play has moments of genuine emotion and insight, it suffers from a somewhat predictable structure and dialogue that occasionally feels forced rather than natural.
The well-acted play, directed by Kenny Leon (Fences), is more like a TV soap opera, with predictable outcomes.
